note: Element definitions live in data, not code. Adding an element means editing this file (spec 3.2). Ids are declared here and are permanent: they are baked into saves and world hashes, so reordering this list must never change behaviour. Id 0 is reserved for empty space.
valueNote: `value` is what a cell is worth to a press, in points. A press takes only what has value, so zero also means the machine ignores it entirely and lets it fall through. `currency` marks the element those points are pressed into: currency has no value of its own, so no press ever takes it back, and currency inside a vault is the player's balance. `burnsInto` and `compactsInto` are the two conversions, and deliberately not machines at all. An element that declares `burnsInto` becomes that product wherever it is at or above its own `ignitionPoint`, with `flammability` as the chance per tick, so dwell time in the heat sets the rate. An element that declares `compactsInto` becomes that product wherever the column standing on it weighs at least `compactionLoad`, with `hardness` as the resistance, so depth sets the rate. Both read a physical quantity the world already has, which is the whole point: the burner and the compactor used to do these jobs and were deleted.
heatNote: `melting_point`/`boiling_point` are Kelvin; `thermal_conductivity` decides how fast a cell trades heat with whatever touches it (spec 5.3) — a heater is the source, everything else just conducts. `meltsInto`/`boilsInto` name what this becomes once its own temperature reaches the matching point; absent means nothing does, which is still true of most of the roster. `condensesInto`/`freezesInto` are the same transitions run backwards, and reuse the same two points rather than declaring thresholds of their own: a gas condenses below its boiling point, a liquid freezes below its melting point. Heating is checked hottest-first, so something hot enough to boil never gets stuck being evaluated as merely melted; cooling is checked nearest-first, so a very cold gas becomes liquid before it becomes solid instead of skipping a state. The comparisons are asymmetric on purpose — `>=` going up, `<` coming down — so a cell parked exactly on a threshold settles on one identity instead of flipping between two every tick.

elements.note: The player's building material: everything hand-drawn is made of this. Painted industrial yellow rather than the grey it started as, and with almost no colour variance — variance reads as grain, which is right for sand and wrong for something manufactured. A flat panel next to speckled powder is most of what makes it look built. Named `structure` (it was `wall`), because it is floors, chutes and machine housings far more often than it is a wall.
elements.name: structure

elements.note: Currency, and matter like everything else. A press turns product into nuggets; a nugget only counts as money once a vault is holding it (spec 5.1). Denser than anything else here, because it is gold — it sinks through water to the bottom of a vault.
elements.name: gold

elements.note: The byproduct of pressing. Denser than sand and wet sand, so it settles below them in a mixed pile rather than mixing back in; far short of gold, so it never buries a nugget. Burns into burntResidue (spec 5.3), but nothing converts it on demand: it burns where it is hot enough, and `flammability` is the chance per tick that it does. How long a cell spends hot is therefore what decides throughput, which makes residence time a consequence of the layout rather than a machine's setting (spec 3.3). Ignites well clear of water's 373K, so a burn run and a wash cannot share a space, and well below its own 1500K melting point, so it always burns rather than melting.
elements.name: residue

elements.note: The next stage: what residue leaves behind once it has burned. Denser again — burning drives off what was loose in it. Compacts into fuel under enough weight, and nothing converts it on demand: `compactionLoad` is the summed density of the column standing on it, so roughly 23 cells of its own kind — about two and a half tiles — before anything happens at all, and past that the rate climbs with depth. `hardness` is the resistance, which is what stops a soft thing and a hard thing compacting alike.
elements.name: burntResidue

elements.note: The end of the chain so far: nothing burns it yet, and nothing spends it. A generic heater is the intended consumer (spec 5.3), not one machine built just for this.
elements.name: fuel

elements.note: Not matter the player ever sees fall or pile up — it is what `World::place` fills a belt's own footprint with (spec 4.1), so gravity holds cargo up on it the same way it holds anything up on solid ground. Solid, so it already never moves; the density is absurd anyway, purely as a second guarantee against ever being displaced. `internal` marks it machine structure rather than material: it hides the row from any player-facing element picker, and the sim reads it too — nothing that carries cargo will carry structure, or a belt whose carry row crossed another machine's body would drag that machine apart a cell at a time.
elements.name: beltStructure

elements.note: A belt chassis that conducts. Everything `beltStructure` is — solid, absurdly dense, never displaced, `internal` so no picker offers it — with the one field inverted: 2.0 against beltStructure's 0.0, well above any material that will ride on it. That inversion is the whole mechanic. Cargo rests on the row directly above a belt's body (`convey_one`), so a run built from this heats what it carries while carrying it, and belt length becomes dwell time. A plain belt is then the deliberately insulated choice rather than the only one. Conducts along itself fast enough that a heater anywhere against the run warms all of it; `heat.rs` takes the *worse* conductor of any touching pair, so ordinary structure at 0.15 still contains the leak.
elements.name: kilnStructure

elements.note: What sand becomes past its melting point (spec 5.3) — a real liquid immediately, not a dead end: it flows and settles like any other liquid the moment it exists. Nothing consumes it yet, the same shape residue and burntResidue shipped in before their own machines existed.
elements.name: moltenSand

elements.note: Boiled water, and the first gas the simulation has ever had — `State::Gas` was an empty arm waiting for exactly this. The lowest conductivity on the roster, and that is the interesting number: heat moves between two cells at the lower of their two conductivities, so steam sheds warmth to a cold ceiling slowly enough to linger as a visible cloud before it condenses and rains back down. Real steam conducts poorly too, so the legible answer and the physical one agree. Density 1 makes it the lightest thing there is, which is the whole of why it rises — nothing names steam in the movement rules.
elements.name: steam

elements.note: What molten sand sets into once it drops back below its melting point, and the first thing heat has ever produced that the player keeps. A solid, so it holds a shape: pour molten sand along a channel, let it cool, and the shape it stopped in is the shape you get. `meltsInto` sends it back to molten, so glass and molten sand are a stable pair — sand melts into the loop once and never comes back out of it, which is what makes melting an upgrade rather than a round trip.
elements.name: glass

reactions.note: Spec 5.3's worked example. Both cells become product, so a reaction changes composition without changing how many cells hold matter.
